FIND: In section 3, EN-11 calculates the elastic modulus E by dividing the ultimate stress (506.67 MPa) by the strain recorded at the same instant (2.410 x 10^-3). This is a fundamental physics error. The elastic modulus is the slope of the linear elastic region. The ultimate stress occurs far beyond the yield point (nominal yield is 275 MPa), in the plastic deformation region.
FOLLOW: The derived modulus E = 210.24 GPa is a secant modulus at the ultimate tensile strength, not the elastic modulus. The text uses this invalid derivation to conclude that the material's elastic modulus is within 3% of the nominal 210 GPa, and therefore "no adjustment to the deflection calculations is warranted." This false validation could mask a batch of steel with an incorrect actual elastic modulus, leading to unsafe deflections in the gantry and mezzanine.
ANALYSE: HARD constraint (Physics/Materials Science). The elastic modulus $E$ is defined only in the linear elastic regime (Hooke's Law: $\sigma = E \epsilon$). The ultimate tensile stress (506.67 MPa) is significantly higher than the yield stress (275 MPa), meaning the material has undergone plastic deformation. The ratio of ultimate stress to its corresponding strain is the secant modulus at UTS, which is physically distinct from the elastic modulus. CONFIRMED.

The result lies within plus or minus 3 per cent of the nominal 210 GPa used in section 2, which is the acceptance band this reference applies, and so no adjustment to the deflection calculations is warranted.

A valid determination of E requires extracting the slope from the linear elastic portion of the coupon test data; until this is done, the validation of the 210 GPa nominal value remains incomplete.

FINDING_ID: F009
SEVERITY: 0.85
FLAW_CLASS: 1
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.3
FIND: In section 8, EN-42 performs a least-squares regression of log10 N on linear stress amplitude (S) to derive a fatigue curve. This implies an exponential fatigue model ($N = C \cdot 10^{k S}$). Standard fatigue models for steel (such as the Basquin equation and Eurocode 3) follow a power law ($N \cdot S^m = C$), which requires regressing log10 N on log10 S.
FOLLOW: The fitted line is "loaded into the detail-category assessment sheet" for interpolation. Because an exponential curve has a different shape than a power-law curve, interpolating fatigue life using the linear-log regression will yield incorrect allowable cycle counts for intermediate stress amplitudes, potentially leading to premature fatigue failure of the gantry or mezzanine components.
ANALYSE: HARD constraint (Physics/Mathematics). Fatigue S-N curves in the high-cycle regime are linear in log-log space, not linear-log space. Regressing $\log_{10} N$ against linear $S$ yields a slope of -0.01217, but this model fundamentally misrepresents the physics of fatigue crack growth (Paris' Law), which integrates to a power-law S-N relationship. CONFIRMED.
